title: Cosima Labs — Dedicated Capacity ramp & multi-tenant guardrails intake
summary: Initial discovery for Cosima's production inference plan. They want reserved GPU capacity with strong isolation between customers, predictable latency at peak, and a burst/fallback strategy to cover unpredictable demand spikes. Key asks: sizing model, isolation topology options (dedicated pools vs soft-tenancy), prewarm/warm pool behaviour, KMS/SSO integrations and SOC2 evidence. Next step: Redwood to run a short pilot (2 weeks) + pricing workbook and security brief.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey, everyone thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Luis is our SE. Quick intros?
[00:12] Priya Nair: Hi I'm Priya, Head of ML at Cosima. We've got Noah in SRE and Ethan on platform. Sofia's jumping on in a bit.
[00:20] Luis Ortega: Hi all, Luis here, I'm gonna focus on infra/ops questions today.
[00:28] Ethan Brooks: Ethan, DevOps, we run most of our inference on managed cloud clusters today.
[00:35] Maya Chen: Great, rough agenda — confirm workloads, discuss Dedicated vs Private, talk isolation and burst patterns, then next steps.
[00:44] Priya Nair: Quick context — we're building a multi-tenant doc understanding product, qps is spiky; typical baseline 400 rps, but marketing campaigns push to 2.2k for short windows. Latency target is p95 < 220ms for small-chat style tasks, and we need strong tenant separation because some customers are regulated.
[01:05] Luis Ortega: Okay, is your current model family mostly open weights or are you using private models?
[01:12] Priya Nair: We're on a mix — open Llama-3 forks for general tasks and a couple of finetuned private models for sensitive clients.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Got it. From Redwood side we usually recommend Dedicated reserved pools for predictable baseline and a warm/burst layer for spikes. Two main isolation patterns: 1) per-tenant isolated nodes (physical or node-pinning), 2) soft-tenancy with strict cgroup and network segmentation.
[01:40] Ethan Brooks: What's the blast radius difference? Curious about noisy neighbor risk.
[01:45] Luis Ortega: If you pin tenants to nodes — blast radius is lower but utilization drops. Soft-tenancy is higher utilization but you need stronger preemption/fairshare and a warm pool for prewarmed models.
[01:58] Priya Nair: We're leaning towards stronger isolation; regulation customers require logical separation and audit logs.
[02:05] Maya Chen: Makes sense. On encryption/keys — we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM), full audit trail and key rotation. We can share SOC2 docs and our private deployment checklist.
[02:18] Noah Park: How does failover work if reserved nodes are saturated? Say we get an unexpected 10x spike for 6 minutes — what's the fallback?
[02:27] Luis Ortega: Typical design: primary reserved pool handles baseline. For spikes we use a warm pool (lighter-weight prewarmed nodes) to absorb bursts. If that saturates, we auto-failover to either a cheaper quantized model variant or to a hosted fallback region — controlled by routing policy. You can set policies: prefer latency, prefer cost, or prefer only private.
[02:46] Priya Nair: Hm, switching to quantized model might affect quality; we need to define SLO degradation thresholds.
[02:52] Maya Chen: Absolutely — you can set degradation windows and ML-eval triggers; Redwood Optimize can run prompt-based regressions and alert.
[03:00] Ethan Brooks: Pricing sensitivity — can you give an example unit cost tradeoff between dedicated nodes vs warm pool vs hosted fallback?
[03:08] Maya Chen: We'll send the workbook but at a high level dedicated reserved nodes give lowest per-token cost at steady state. Warm pool costs a bit more per unit because of prewarmed memory residency but avoids cold start latency. Hosted fallback is cheapest to operate but can be higher latency and potential data residency concerns.
[03:24] Priya Nair: For data residency we need to ensure region-specific isolation — can warm pools be region pinned?
[03:30] Luis Ortega: Yes, pools are region-specific and you can restrict routing to that region.
[03:34] [crosstalk] Sofia Romero: Sorry I'm late — quick catch up?
[03:40] Maya Chen: Quick summary — Cosima baseline 400 rps, spikes 2.2k, needs per-tenant separation for regulated customers, wants p95 < 220ms. We'll go into topology options.
[03:55] Sofia Romero: Ok realtime constraint — our SLAs are customer-facing, we can't exceed 250ms p95 or we pay credits.
[04:02] Luis Ortega: For that you likely need a combination: dedicated hot pool sized for your p95 target at baseline plus a warm pool to absorb spikes with prewarmed KV-caches. Also ephemeral async fallback for non-critical requests.
[04:18] Ethan Brooks: How does KV cache behave across model variants? If you route to a quantized variant, do you lose the KV cache warm state?
[04:26] Luis Ortega: If the variant is architecture-compatible and same tokenizer, we can share KV cache across certain families. If not compatible, we fall back to prefix caching and warm-start sequences, which costs a little more. Sometimes the transcript engine may show "kay vee cash" in logs — that was funny — but it's basically token cache.
[04:44] Priya Nair: Deployment modes — what's the lift to get Private (VPC) vs Hosted + Dedicated?
[04:51] Maya Chen: Hosted + Dedicated is quickest: you get reserved pools in our managed plane, with tenant isolation options. Private (VPC or on-prem) requires a short onboarding: networking, KMS integration, and an air-gapped setup if needed — typically 4-8 weeks depending on approvals.
[05:06] Noah Park: For our security team, we need SSO (SAML), RBAC, and syslog streaming. Is that standard?
[05:13] Amira Patel: Yes — SSO/SAML, role-based access controls, audit logs, and log-forwarding to your SIEM are standard in enterprise tiers. We can provide log schemas.
[05:21] Priya Nair: What's your experience on prewarming models for sudden marketing bursts? Any operational gotchas?
[05:28] Luis Ortega: Common gotchas: (1) model prewarm churn — if you prewarm too many distinct models you'll hurt utilization; (2) prewarm timing — shorter bursts need faster prewarm strategies (warm pool or model striping); (3) stateful session routing — K/V transfer needs compatibility. We usually suggest a small warm pool with prioritized warm models based on traffic heuristics.
[05:47] Ethan Brooks: Can warm pools be auto-scaled based on short-term rate of change?
[05:52] Luis Ortega: Yes — autoscaling policies can be rate-of-change aware. You'll set thresholds like 3-second sustained growth triggers and backing cooldowns to avoid flapping.
[06:01] Priya Nair: Ok, let's talk numbers. If our baseline is 400 rps with 30k tokens/minute and spikes up to 2.2k for 8-12 minute windows, what would you recommend for reserved capacity?
[06:12] Maya Chen: Roughly you'd reserve capacity to cover 60-70% of expected peak to keep costs reasonable and lean on warm pools for short bursts. We'll need a request profile (seq lengths, batching headroom, tokens per request) to calculate exact GPU counts. Can you share a 48h trace?
[06:28] Priya Nair: Yes we'll share the traces.
[06:31] Sofia Romero: On auditability — we need immutable audit trail for model version, prompts and who accessed. Can Redwood provide that without storing PII?
[06:40] Amira Patel: Yes — we support token-level logs with redaction options. We can stream sanitized telemetry to your audit bucket. Private deployments let you keep logs within your environment.
[06:50] Ethan Brooks: Network ingress/egress — if we go Private in our VPC, do we need to open outbound egress to Redwood control plane?
[06:57] Luis Ortega: For VPC Private mode, control plane endpoints can be peered; we provide options for minimal metadata calls, and you can put all sensitive traffic over private links.
[07:06] Priya Nair: Anything else that usually surprises customers when migrating from managed endpoints to reserved dedicated capacity?
[07:12] Maya Chen: Two things: first, the ops behavior — you trade some elasticity for predictability; second, observability configuration — with Dedicated it's critical to tune tracing and cost attribution per model route.
[07:24] Noah Park: SLA questions — do you provide latency SLO guarantees for reserved pools?
[07:29] Maya Chen: We have SLA tiers; for Dedicated we can commit to uptime and p95 latency windows per contract. We'll include target numbers in a draft SOW.
[07:38] Priya Nair: On fallback quality — if you route to a hosted fallback model, what are privacy guarantees?
[07:44] Amira Patel: Hosted fallback respects data handling policies, but for regulated customers we recommend Private or Dedicated with private control plane. We'll mark fallback routes as disabled for those tenants if necessary.
[07:55] Ethan Brooks: Do you offer hybrid routing — like tenant uses Dedicated for sensitive calls and Hosted for telemetry/analytics?
[08:01] Luis Ortega: Yes — routing policy rules can partition by route, tenant, or tag, so you can send sensitive requests to Dedicated and analytics/aggregation to hosted cheaper endpoints.
[08:12] Priya Nair: That's useful. For the pilot we want to validate prewarm times and failover behavior under synthetic spikes. What's realistic scope for a 2-week pilot?
[08:20] Maya Chen: 2-week pilot scope: (1) provision a small dedicated pool sized to your baseline, (2) configure a warm pool and autoscale policies, (3) run 3 spike scenarios (short burst, long sustained, model-switching), (4) gather latency/cost/quality metrics and run Redwood Optimize suggestions. We'll produce a summary with suggested reserve sizes.
[08:40] Sofia Romero: Who signs the pilot? Is there any commitment?
[08:44] Maya Chen: Pilot is low-commitment; we ask for a sandbox account and a small play credit to cover reserved prewarm hours. We'll send terms.
[08:51] Priya Nair: Timeline — we'd like pilot started within 2 weeks. Can you match that?
[08:55] Maya Chen: Yes, assuming we get the traffic traces and a sandbox VPC or access keys. We'll need platform contacts and approvals.
[09:03] Ethan Brooks: Integration checklist — what do you need from our side?
[09:07] Luis Ortega: 1) 48-72h request traces, 2) model artifacts/weights or names, 3) a list of regulated tenants and their region/residency needs, 4) network contact for VPC peering or IP allowlists.
[09:20] Priya Nair: We'll share traces and tenant list by EOD Thursday.
[09:24] Maya Chen: Great. Action items we'll confirm.
[09:28] Amira Patel: One quick note on quantization — for some of your finetuned models we can recommend 4-bit quantized variants that keep quality within tolerance. We'll run a small eval during pilot.
[09:39] Priya Nair: Good. Any concerns about warm pool costs creeping up? We need cost guardrails.
[09:44] Luis Ortega: You can set budget caps and scale down policies, plus per-tenant budgets so one customer can't blow the whole pool.
[09:52] Noah Park: For disaster scenarios — if a whole AZ goes down, what's the cross-region failover plan?
[09:58] Maya Chen: Multi-region reserved pools are common; you'd replicate a hot subset in another region or rely on hosted fallback for short windows. We can discuss RPO/RTO targets in the SOW.
[10:09] Sofia Romero: Ok, I'm convinced this is workable. Send the security docs and the pricing workbook and we'll triage internally.
[10:16] Maya Chen: Will do. We'll share the SOC2/ISO brief, architecture playbook, and a pricing workbook with a recommended reserved node configuration. Also attaching the benchmark spreadsheet we run for p95 sizing.
[10:27] Priya Nair: Great. Quick final Q — any caveats on model logging and retention with Private? We might need 7 year retention for audit.
[10:35] Amira Patel: Private deployments can meet long retention via your S3/archival policies; we can export logs and lifecycle them to Glacier or your on-prem archives.
[10:44] Ethan Brooks: Perfect.
[10:46] Maya Chen: Recap and next steps coming now in the action items. Thanks everyone.
[10:52] [meeting ends]
